title: Grief that teaches nothing
hook: after his son Waldo died, Emerson wrote that grief could teach him nothing (Experience, 1844)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the only gift: Emerson calling rings and jewels apologies for gifts. Your line was a portion of myself. What did you start making, and for whom? Day one thousand two hundred five.

"Where do we find ourselves?" That's how Emerson opens his essay Experience. Not with an answer, but with a fog. He says we wake and find ourselves on a stair, with stairs below that we seem to have climbed and stairs above going up out of sight. It's a disoriented beginning, and a little further in comes something some readers hear behind the whole essay. Emerson's young son, Waldo, had died. And Emerson, a writer known for lifting people up, says something that can still unsettle a reader: that grief had not taught him anything. Today, that hard honesty.
screen: `WHERE DO WE FIND OURSELVES?` → `ON A STAIR, IN A FOG.` → `HIS SON HAD DIED.`

segments.voice: First, what he says about the loss. Emerson writes that losing his son felt like losing a beautiful estate, and no more. That he cannot get it nearer to him. It's a startling way to put it, almost flat, and some readers find it cold. Others hear a man too stunned to make the loss into anything. Second, the line itself. "I grieve that grief can teach me nothing, nor carry me one step into real nature." Notice what he's grieving. Not only his son, but the fact that the grief doesn't open anything up. No lesson. No deeper insight. It doesn't carry him anywhere. Third, why that matters. People in sorrow are sometimes told that everything happens for a reason, or that this will make them stronger. Some find comfort in that. Emerson, at least here, won't say it. He refuses to dress a loss up as a lesson. There's a kind of respect in that, for his son and for anyone whose grief hasn't turned into wisdom and may never. It gives permission for a loss to simply be a loss. Fourth, he keeps writing. The essay doesn't end in the fog. Emerson goes on, page after page, to ask how to live in the days we actually have, and he lands on filling the hour, living the present well. He doesn't claim the grief taught him that. He just keeps walking up the stair. Sometimes that's all there is to do with a sorrow that makes no sense: carry it, and keep going.
screen: `A BEAUTIFUL ESTATE, AND NO MORE.` · `GRIEF CAN TEACH ME NOTHING.` · `NO LESSON DRESSED ONTO IT.` · `HE KEEPS WALKING UP THE STAIR.` · then, large: `IT TAUGHT NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a grief that made no sense, if one is there. Settle, and let the breath be slow. If a loss comes to mind, a person, a place, a hope, let it be here without asking it to mean anything. No lesson, no silver lining. Just hold it for a few breaths, the way you might sit beside someone without talking. If nothing comes, or if today it's too much, simply rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Grief that teaches nothing. Emerson, in Experience, after his son's death: grieving that grief could not carry him one step further. Today's word.
Your line: it taught nothing. Today, if someone near you is grieving, try not to hand them a reason. Just stay near. Day one thousand two hundred five.

howItsDone: Readers often return to this passage in Experience when grieving, finding in it permission not to turn a loss into a lesson.
